name: Baekje
summary: One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, in the south-west. It had the largest population of the three and passed Buddhism and Chinese learning on to Japan.

location.value: South-western Korea; at its 4th-century peak most of the western peninsula.

terrain.value: Fertile plains and river valleys along Korea’s south-west coast.

climate.value: Temperate, with monsoon rains in summer and cold winters.

resources.value: Good rice land and access to the Yellow Sea for trade.

disasters.value: Unknown in detail; chronicles mention droughts and floods.

population.value: About 3.8 million (760,000 households), the largest of the three kingdoms.

urbanisation.value: Capitals at Wiryeseong (Seoul), Ungjin and Sabi.

migration.value: Many Baekje people moved to Japan, especially after 660, bringing skills and learning.

economicBase.value: The page mentions maritime trade with China and Japan and cultural exchange but gives no details on farming or taxes.

tradeRoutes.value: Sea links with southern Chinese dynasties and with Japan (Yamato).

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; royal tombs held gold crowns and fine objects.

moneyAndTax.value: Taxes paid in rice, cloth and labour.

inequality.value: Eight great aristocratic families held most power.

governmentType.value: Monarchy with aristocratic clans; government organised into ministries modelled on China.

keyRulers.value: Onjo founded the kingdom (18 BCE, per the Samguk sagi); Geunchogo (346–375) expanded north and annexed the remaining Mahan states; Seong (523–554) moved the capital to Sabi and was killed fighting Silla; Uija (641–660) was the last king. Muryeong is not covered in the part read.

succession.value: Hereditary in the royal Buyeo family.

institutions.value: Six ministries and a ranked officialdom modelled partly on China.

stability.value: Goguryeo captured the capital near present-day Seoul in 475, forcing a move south.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalries between aristocratic families and the king are recorded.

armyAndTech.value: Fortresses and armies drawn from farmers; Japanese troops sometimes helped.

majorWars.value: Geunchogo defeated Goguryeo at Pyongyang in 371; Seoul fell to Goguryeo in 475; Baekje and Silla alternately fought and allied; Tang China and Silla defeated Baekje in 660.

territoryChange.value: Lost the Han River valley in 475 and again to Silla in 553.

alliancesRivals.value: Alternately fought and allied with Goguryeo and Silla.

inventions.value: Skilled bronze casting and brick tomb building.

scienceEducation.value: Baekje scholars and craftsmen took Chinese learning, Buddhism and writing to Japan.

openness.value: A bridge between China and Japan, passing on writing, Buddhism and crafts.

communicationTransport.value: Sea routes to southern China and Japan; river boats on the Geum River; post roads between fortresses.

religion.value: Buddhism was introduced and accepted in 384; King Seong made it the state religion in 528.

languageWriting.value: Records were written in Chinese characters; the Baekje language is little known.

artsArchitecture.value: The gilt-bronze incense burner of Baekje and the tomb of King Muryeong.

socialStructure.value: Royal family, aristocrats, farmers and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: The royal family claimed descent from Buyeo, like Goguryeo.

dailyLife.value: Thatched and tiled wooden houses; rice, barley, fish and seaweed; hemp and silk clothing.

neighbours.value: Goguryeo, Silla, Gaya, Japan and Chinese dynasties.

ideasReligions.value: Sent Buddhist images and texts to Japan, traditionally dated 552 (or 538).

colonisation.value: None; it had close ties with Japan but no colonies.

riseSignals.value: Founded by Onjo in 18 BCE near modern Seoul.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Baekje (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

peakPeriod.value: The 4th century under King Geunchogo, controlling most of the western peninsula.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Baekje (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

declineSignals.value: Lost the Han river region to Goguryeo (475) and later faced a Silla–Tang alliance.

outcome.value: Conquered by Silla and Tang China in 660; a revival attempt with Japanese help failed in 663.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Baekje (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Based on the Samguk sagi (12th century) and archaeology.
